No overclaims.How does the atom partition alpha ab relate to the transposition tau
The atom partition $$\alpha_{ab}$$ is the **partition-lattice atom representing the bare identification $$a\sim b$$**. The transposition $$\tau=(a\,b)$$ is a permutation of the underlying set; it acts on partitions by relabeling, and its dynamical join
$$
J_\tau(\Pi)=\Pi\vee\tau(\Pi)
$$
is generally **not** equal to $$\Pi\vee\alpha_{ab}$$.
The precise relationship is:
$$
\alpha_{ab}
\quad\text{is the least partition that forces }a\sim b,
$$
whereas
$$
\tau(\Pi)
\quad\text{moves the existing relation }E_\Pi
\text{ by conjugation.}
$$
The atom is a fixed lattice element; the transposition is an automorphism of the partition lattice.
## Atom partition
Let $$X$$ be finite and $$a\ne b\in X$$. Define
$$
\alpha_{ab}
=
\bigl\{\{a,b\}\bigr\}
\cup
\bigl\{\{x\}:x\in X\setminus\{a,b\}\bigr\}.
$$
Its equivalence relation is
$$
E_{\alpha_{ab}}
=
\Delta_X\cup\{(a,b),(b,a)\},
$$
where $$\Delta_X=\{(x,x):x\in X\}$$.
Under refinement order, $$\alpha_{ab}$$ covers the discrete partition:
$$
\widehat0\lessdot\alpha_{ab}.
$$
That is why it is an atom in $$\Pi(X)$$.
Joining a partition $$\Pi$$ with this atom means:
$$
\Pi\vee\alpha_{ab}
=
\operatorname{Eq}\!\left(
E_\Pi\cup\{(a,b),(b,a)\}
\right).
$$
It has a simple block description:
$$
\Pi\vee\alpha_{ab}
=
\begin{cases}
\Pi,&a\sim_\Pi b,\$$4pt]
\text{$$\Pi$$ with $$[a]\_\Pi$$ and $$[b]\_\Pi$$ merged},&a\not\sim_\Pi b.
\end{cases}
$$
So $$\Pi\vee\alpha_{ab}$$ is always the elementary merge induced by forcibly adding the one edge $$a\!-\!b$$.
## Transposition action
The transposition
$$
\tau=(a\,b)
$$
acts on partitions by transporting every block:
$$
\tau(\Pi)=\{\tau(B):B\in\Pi\}.
$$
At the relation level:
$$
E_{\tau(\Pi)}
=
\tau E_\Pi\tau^{-1},
$$
meaning
$$
x\sim_{\tau(\Pi)}y
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\tau(x)\sim_\Pi\tau(y),
$$
since $$\tau^{-1}=\tau$$.
Thus the exact formula for the dynamical join is:
$$
\boxed{
E_{J_\tau(\Pi)}
=
\operatorname{Eq}\!\left(
E_\Pi\cup\tau E_\Pi\tau
\right).
}
$$
This is the only universal equivalence-closure formula for the transposition operator.
The distinction is fundamental:

| Object | Mathematical type | Action |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $$\alpha_{ab}$$ | Fixed atom of the partition lattice | Directly imposes $$a\sim b$$ |
| $$\tau=(a\,b)$$ | Permutation of $$X$$ | Relabels an entire partition relation |
| $$\Pi\vee\alpha_{ab}$$ | Elementary join/merge | Adds the pair $$(a,b)$$ |
| $$J_\tau(\Pi)=\Pi\vee\tau(\Pi)$$ | Dynamical join | Joins $$\Pi$$ with its transposed image |

Partitions and equivalence relations are equivalent descriptions of the same objects: every partition induces the “same block” equivalence relation, and every equivalence relation yields its class partition.[1][2]
## Why they differ
The atom $$\alpha_{ab}$$ has one job:
$$
a\leftrightarrow b.
$$
The image partition $$\tau(\Pi)$$ instead modifies the memberships of $$a$$ and $$b$$ in **all existing blocks**:
$$
\tau(A)=
\begin{cases}
(A\setminus\{a\})\cup\{b\},&a\in A,\ b\notin A,\\
(A\setminus\{b\})\cup\{a\},&b\in A,\ a\notin A,\\
A,&\{a,b\}\subseteq A\text{ or }\{a,b\}\cap A=\varnothing.
\end{cases}
$$
Therefore $$\tau(\Pi)$$ need not contain a relation edge connecting $$a$$ to $$b$$. In fact it contains that edge exactly when one of the original $$a$$- or $$b$$-blocks has sufficient nontrivial support to create an overlap path in the join.
The most important counterexample is the discrete partition:
$$
\Pi=\widehat0
=
\bigl\{\{a\},\{b\}\bigr\}
\cup
\bigl\{\{x\}:x\notin\{a,b\}\bigr\}.
$$
Because permuting singleton blocks leaves the unordered partition unchanged:
$$
\tau(\widehat0)=\widehat0.
$$
Hence:
$$
J_\tau(\widehat0)
=
\widehat0\vee\widehat0
=
\widehat0.
$$
But:
$$
\widehat0\vee\alpha_{ab}
=
\alpha_{ab}.
$$
So:
$$
\boxed{
J_\tau(\widehat0)\ne\widehat0\vee\alpha_{ab}.
}
$$
This proves that a transposition action is not “join with its atom.”
## Exact comparison theorem
Let:
$$
A=[a]_\Pi,
\qquad
B=[b]_\Pi.
$$
Then:
$$
\boxed{
J_\tau(\Pi)\le \Pi\vee\alpha_{ab}
}
$$
in refinement order.
Equivalently:
$$
E_{J_\tau(\Pi)}
\subseteq
E_{\Pi\vee\alpha_{ab}}.
$$
### Proof
Let:
$$
C:=E_{\Pi\vee\alpha_{ab}}
=
\operatorname{Eq}\!\bigl(E_\Pi\cup\{(a,b),(b,a)\}\bigr).
$$
Clearly:
$$
E_\Pi\subseteq C.
$$
For any $$x,y$$ satisfying
$$
x\sim_{\tau(\Pi)}y,
$$
we have:
$$
\tau(x)\sim_\Pi\tau(y).
$$
But in $$C$$, every point is equivalent to its $$\tau$$-image:
$$
x\sim_C\tau(x),
$$
because:
- if $$x\notin\{a,b\}$$, then $$\tau(x)=x$$;
- if $$x=a$$, then $$\tau(x)=b$$, and $$a\sim_C b$$;
- if $$x=b$$, then $$\tau(x)=a$$, and $$b\sim_C a$$.
Hence:
$$
x
\sim_C
\tau(x)
\sim_C
\tau(y)
\sim_C
y.
$$
So:
$$
E_{\tau(\Pi)}\subseteq C.
$$
Since $$C$$ is an equivalence relation containing both $$E_\Pi$$ and $$E_{\tau(\Pi)}$$, it contains their join:
$$
E_{J_\tau(\Pi)}
=
\operatorname{Eq}(E_\Pi\cup E_{\tau(\Pi)})
\subseteq C.
$$
Thus:
$$
\boxed{
J_\tau(\Pi)\le \Pi\vee\alpha_{ab}.
}
$$
$$\square$$
The inequality can be strict only in the singleton-singular case below.
## Exact equality criterion
The comparison sharpens to a complete criterion:
$$
\boxed{
J_\tau(\Pi)=\Pi\vee\alpha_{ab}
\iff
\left(
a\sim_\Pi b
\right)
\ \text{or}\
\left(
[a]_\Pi\setminus\{a\}\ne\varnothing
\right)
\ \text{or}\
\left(
[b]_\Pi\setminus\{b\}\ne\varnothing
\right).
}
$$
Equivalently:
$$
\boxed{
J_\tau(\Pi)\ne\Pi\vee\alpha_{ab}
\iff
[a]_\Pi=\{a\}
\quad\text{and}\quad
[b]_\Pi=\{b\}.
}
$$
### Proof
If $$a\sim_\Pi b$$, then:
$$
\Pi\vee\alpha_{ab}=\Pi.
$$
The block containing both $$a,b$$ is fixed setwise by $$\tau$$, as are all blocks disjoint from $$\{a,b\}$$; hence:
$$
\tau(\Pi)=\Pi,
\qquad
J_\tau(\Pi)=\Pi.
$$
Now suppose:
$$
A\ne B.
$$
If $$A\setminus\{a\}\ne\varnothing$$, choose:
$$
x\in A\setminus\{a\}.
$$
Then:
$$
a\sim_\Pi x,
$$
while:
$$
x\sim_{\tau(\Pi)}b,
$$
because $$x\in\tau(A)$$ and $$b=\tau(a)\in\tau(A)$$. Therefore:
$$
a\sim_{J_\tau(\Pi)} b.
$$
Since $$J_\tau(\Pi)$$ already coarsens $$\Pi$$, once it identifies $$a$$ and $$b$$, it must coarsen the least partition doing so:
$$
\Pi\vee\alpha_{ab}\le J_\tau(\Pi).
$$
Together with the universal reverse comparison:
$$
J_\tau(\Pi)\le\Pi\vee\alpha_{ab},
$$
we obtain equality:
$$
J_\tau(\Pi)=\Pi\vee\alpha_{ab}.
$$
The same proof works if:
$$
B\setminus\{b\}\ne\varnothing.
$$
Finally, if:
$$
A=\{a\},
\qquad
B=\{b\},
$$
then $$\tau$$ merely exchanges two singleton blocks in an unordered block family:
$$
\tau(\Pi)=\Pi.
$$
Thus:
$$
J_\tau(\Pi)=\Pi,
$$
but:
$$
\Pi\vee\alpha_{ab}
$$
strictly merges the two singleton blocks. Equality fails.
This proves the criterion. $$\square$$
## Consequences for $$J_\tau$$
The cleanest exact formula is therefore:
$$
\boxed{
J_\tau(\Pi)=
\begin{cases}
\Pi\vee\alpha_{ab},
& \text{if }[a]_\Pi\ne\{a\}\text{ or }[b]_\Pi\ne\{b\},\$$6pt]
\Pi,
& \text{if }[a]_\Pi=\{a\}\text{ and }[b]_\Pi=\{b\}.
\end{cases}
}
$$
This includes the case $$a\sim_\Pi b$$, because then neither $$a$$- nor $$b$$-class is a singleton unless $$a=b$$, excluded by definition.
Equivalently, defining:
$$
\eta_\Pi(a,b)
=
\begin{cases}
1,&a\not\sim_\Pi b
\text{ and }
\bigl(|[a]_\Pi|>1\text{ or }|[b]_\Pi|>1\bigr),\\
0,&\text{otherwise},
\end{cases}
$$
we obtain:
$$
r(J_\tau(\Pi))-r(\Pi)=\eta_\Pi(a,b),
$$
where $$r(\Pi)=n-|\Pi|$$.
So a transposition can have three qualitative behaviors:

| $$\Pi$$-configuration at $$a,b$$ | $$J_\tau(\Pi)$$ | Rank increase |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $$a,b$$ already in one block | Identity | 0 |
| $$a,b$$ in two singleton blocks | Identity | 0 |
| Distinct blocks, at least one non-singleton | Merge exactly those two blocks | 1 |

This corrected activity indicator—not merely $$a\not\sim_\Pi b$$—is the quantity that must enter any transposition transport or blocker analysis.
## Relation to the graphic atom
In the graphic-matroid realization of the partition lattice, $$\alpha_{ab}$$ corresponds to the rank-one flat generated by the graph edge:
$$
e_{ab}=\{a,b\}
$$
of $$K_n$$.
Thus:
$$
\Pi\vee\alpha_{ab}
$$
is literally closure after adding the fixed edge $$e_{ab}$$ to the graphic flat associated with $$\Pi$$.
By contrast:
$$
J_\tau(\Pi)=\Pi\vee\tau(\Pi)
$$
is the join of a flat with its image under a vertex permutation. It can be viewed as the closure of the union of two edge sets:
$$
F_\Pi\cup\tau(F_\Pi),
$$
rather than as closure after adding one fixed edge.
For a nontrivial $$a$$-block, the symmetric difference between $$F_\Pi$$ and $$\tau(F_\Pi)$$ provides paths that make the effect equivalent to adding $$e_{ab}$$. When both $$a,b$$ are singleton blocks, there are no incident flat edges to transport, so the transposition leaves $$F_\Pi$$ unchanged and contributes no edge.
This is the geometric reason behind the exceptional case.
## V150 impact
The exact safe replacement for the earlier unconditional transposition statement is:
$$
\boxed{
J_{(a\,b)}(\Pi)
=
\Pi\vee\alpha_{ab}
\quad\text{unless }a,b\text{ are distinct singleton blocks of }\Pi.
}
$$
More formally:
$$
\boxed{
J_{(a\,b)}(\Pi)
=
\begin{cases}
\Pi,&[a]_\Pi=\{a\}\text{ and }[b]_\Pi=\{b\},\\
\Pi\vee\alpha_{ab},&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
}
$$
This correction is important for any proposed transposition $$m$$-blocker proof. It does not refute the blocker conjecture or the reported finite census, but it means the correct proof must account explicitly for the inert “two singleton endpoints” case rather than assuming that $$(a\,b)$$ always introduces the atom $$\alpha_{ab}$$.Prove the equivalence closure relation for the transposition operator J
For a transposition $$\tau=(a\,b)$$, the dynamical join operator is exactly the equivalence closure obtained by adjoining the pair $$(a,b)$$ to the partition relation:
$$
\boxed{
E_{J_\tau(\Pi)}
=
\operatorname{Eq}\!\bigl(E_\Pi\cup\{(a,b),(b,a)\}\bigr).
}
$$
Equivalently,
$$
\boxed{
J_\tau(\Pi)=\Pi\vee\alpha_{ab},
}
$$
where $$\alpha_{ab}$$ is the atom partition whose sole nonsingleton block is $$\{a,b\}$$.
This establishes the transposition action in the strongest useful form: $$J_\tau$$ is “join with a fixed atomic equivalence relation,” hence it is extensive, monotone, and join-preserving.
## Definitions
Let $$X$$ be a finite set, $$\Pi$$ a partition of $$X$$, and $$E_\Pi\subseteq X\times X$$ its equivalence relation:
$$
x\,E_\Pi\,y
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x,y\text{ lie in the same }\Pi\text{-block}.
$$
Let
$$
\tau=(a\,b)
$$
be a transposition. The image partition $$\tau(\Pi)$$ has relation
$$
E_{\tau(\Pi)}
=
\tau E_\Pi\tau^{-1},
$$
meaning:
$$
x\,E_{\tau(\Pi)}\,y
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\tau^{-1}(x)\,E_\Pi\,\tau^{-1}(y).
$$
Under refinement order,
$$
\Pi\le\Sigma
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
E_\Pi\subseteq E_\Sigma.
$$
The join is the least equivalence relation containing both:
$$
E_{\Pi\vee\Sigma}
=
\operatorname{Eq}(E_\Pi\cup E_\Sigma),
$$
where $$\operatorname{Eq}$$ denotes reflexive, symmetric, transitive closure. This equivalence-relation realization of the partition-lattice join is standard.[1]
Define:
$$
J_\tau(\Pi):=\Pi\vee\tau(\Pi).
$$
Finally, set:
$$
e_{ab}:=\{(a,b),(b,a)\},
$$
and let
$$
\alpha_{ab}
=
\bigl\{\{a,b\}\bigr\}
\cup
\bigl\{\{x\}:x\in X\setminus\{a,b\}\bigr\}.
$$
Then:
$$
E_{\alpha_{ab}}
=
\Delta_X\cup e_{ab},
$$
where
$$
\Delta_X=\{(x,x):x\in X\}
$$
is the diagonal relation.
## Transposition closure theorem
### Theorem
For every partition $$\Pi$$ of $$X$$,
$$
\boxed{
\Pi\vee\tau(\Pi)
=
\Pi\vee\alpha_{ab}.
}
$$
Equivalently:
$$
\boxed{
\operatorname{Eq}
\bigl(E_\Pi\cup E_{\tau(\Pi)}\bigr)
=
\operatorname{Eq}
\bigl(E_\Pi\cup e_{ab}\bigr).
}
$$
### Proof
Let:
$$
R:=E_\Pi,
\qquad
R^\tau:=E_{\tau(\Pi)}=\tau R\tau^{-1},
$$
and define:
$$
C:=\operatorname{Eq}(R\cup e_{ab}).
$$
We prove:
$$
\operatorname{Eq}(R\cup R^\tau)=C
$$
by proving two inclusions.
### First inclusion
We show:
$$
R^\tau\subseteq C.
$$
Take:
$$
(x,y)\in R^\tau.
$$
By definition of conjugation:
$$
(\tau(x),\tau(y))\in R.
$$
Because $$\tau$$ only swaps $$a$$ and $$b$$, for every $$z\in X$$:
$$
z\,C\,\tau(z).
$$
Indeed:
- If $$z\notin\{a,b\}$$, then $$\tau(z)=z$$, and reflexivity gives $$z\,C\,\tau(z)$$.
- If $$z=a$$, then $$\tau(z)=b$$, and $$(a,b)\in e_{ab}\subseteq C$$.
- If $$z=b$$, then $$\tau(z)=a$$, and $$(b,a)\in e_{ab}\subseteq C$$.
Since:
$$
(\tau(x),\tau(y))\in R\subseteq C,
$$
transitivity of $$C$$ yields:
$$
x\,C\,\tau(x)
\,C\,
\tau(y)
\,C\,
y.
$$
Hence:
$$
x\,C\,y.
$$
Therefore:
$$
R^\tau\subseteq C.
$$
Since $$R\subseteq C$$ as well:
$$
R\cup R^\tau\subseteq C.
$$
Because $$C$$ is an equivalence relation:
$$
\operatorname{Eq}(R\cup R^\tau)\subseteq C.
$$
Thus:
$$
\boxed{
E_{J_\tau(\Pi)}
=
\operatorname{Eq}(R\cup R^\tau)
\subseteq
\operatorname{Eq}(R\cup e_{ab}).
}
$$
### Second inclusion
We show:
$$
e_{ab}\subseteq\operatorname{Eq}(R\cup R^\tau).
$$
Since $$\tau(a)=b$$, reflexivity of $$R$$ gives:
$$
(a,a)\in R.
$$
Conjugating by $$\tau$$:
$$
(\tau(a),\tau(a))
=
(b,b)
\in R^\tau.
$$
That observation alone does not connect $$a$$ and $$b$$, so the real argument is block-based.
Let:
$$
A=[a]_\Pi,
\qquad
B=[b]_\Pi.
$$
If:
$$
A=B,
$$
then:
$$
(a,b)\in R\subseteq\operatorname{Eq}(R\cup R^\tau).
$$
Now suppose:
$$
A\ne B.
$$
Because $$a\in A$$, we have:
$$
(a,a)\in R,
$$
and because $$\tau(a)=b$$, the image under $$\tau$$ of the block $$A$$ is:
$$
\tau(A)=(A\setminus\{a\})\cup\{b\}.
$$
Likewise:
$$
\tau(B)=(B\setminus\{b\})\cup\{a\}.
$$
The essential connectivity is obtained through the two original blocks and their images:
- $$a$$ belongs to $$A$$ and to $$\tau(B)$$;
- $$b$$ belongs to $$B$$ and to $$\tau(A)$$.
However, this alone still does not imply $$a\sim b$$ in every arbitrary partition. The correct proof instead uses the defining relation of the join of the *partitions* and the fact that $$\Pi$$ and $$\tau(\Pi)$$ are related by swapping the membership of $$a,b$$.
A direct path is:
$$
a
\sim_{\tau(\Pi)}
x
\sim_{\Pi}
b
$$
only when an appropriate $$x$$ exists, so a purported universal proof by this route is invalid.
Indeed, the claimed identity
$$
\Pi\vee\tau(\Pi)=\Pi\vee\alpha_{ab}
$$
is **false in general**.
## Counterexample to the claimed identity
Take:
$$
X=\{a,b,c,d\},
$$
with:
$$
\Pi=\bigl\{\{a,c\},\{b,d\}\bigr\},
\qquad
\tau=(a\,b).
$$
Then:
$$
\tau(\Pi)
=
\bigl\{\{b,c\},\{a,d\}\bigr\}.
$$
The join $$\Pi\vee\tau(\Pi)$$ is indiscrete:
$$
\Pi\vee\tau(\Pi)=\{\{a,b,c,d\}\},
$$
because the block-overlap graph is connected:
$$
a\sim_\Pi c\sim_{\tau(\Pi)} b\sim_\Pi d\sim_{\tau(\Pi)} a.
$$
On the other hand:
$$
\Pi\vee\alpha_{ab}
=
\{\{a,b,c,d\}\}
$$
in this example as well, so it does not refute the identity.
A smaller test is needed.
Take:
$$
X=\{a,b,c\},
\qquad
\Pi=\{\{a,c\},\{b\}\},
\qquad
\tau=(a\,b).
$$
Then:
$$
\tau(\Pi)=\{\{b,c\},\{a\}\}.
$$
Both joins are indiscrete:
$$
\Pi\vee\tau(\Pi)
=
\Pi\vee\alpha_{ab}
=
\{\{a,b,c\}\}.
$$
In fact the first inclusion proves:
$$
\Pi\vee\tau(\Pi)\le\Pi\vee\alpha_{ab}.
$$
The reverse inclusion holds because $$a$$ and $$b$$ always become connected in $$\Pi\vee\tau(\Pi)$$:
- If $$a\sim_\Pi b$$, this is immediate.
- If they are distinct, consider the $$\Pi$$-block $$A$$ containing $$a$$. Its $$\tau$$-image contains $$b$$. The two blocks $$A\in\Pi$$ and $$\tau(A)\in\tau(\Pi)$$ intersect in $$A\setminus\{a\}$$ only if $$A$$ has another point; if $$A=\{a\}$$, it does not.
So the singleton case still requires care. For:
$$
\Pi=\{\{a\},\{b\},\{c\}\},
$$
we have:
$$
\tau(\Pi)=\Pi,
$$
and therefore:
$$
J_\tau(\Pi)=\Pi,
$$
whereas:
$$
\Pi\vee\alpha_{ab}
=
\{\{a,b\},\{c\}\}.
$$
Therefore:
$$
\boxed{
J_\tau(\Pi)\ne\Pi\vee\alpha_{ab}
}
$$
for the discrete partition.
This is decisive.
## Correct equivalence-closure formula
The exact universal formula is simply:
$$
\boxed{
E_{J_\tau(\Pi)}
=
\operatorname{Eq}\!\left(
E_\Pi\cup\tau E_\Pi\tau^{-1}
\right).
}
$$
The transposition action cannot generally be replaced by “adjoin the pair $$(a,b)$$.”
The actual block behavior is:
$$
J_\tau(\Pi)
=
\Pi\vee\tau(\Pi),
$$
where $$\tau(\Pi)$$ swaps the membership of the two distinguished points $$a,b$$, leaving all other elements in their corresponding image blocks.
## Correct transposition block formula
Let:
$$
A=[a]_\Pi,\qquad B=[b]_\Pi.
$$
There are three cases.
### Case 1: $$A=B$$
Then $$\tau$$ preserves the block $$A$$ as a set:
$$
\tau(A)=A.
$$
Every other block is fixed by $$\tau$$. Hence:
$$
\tau(\Pi)=\Pi,
$$
and:
$$
\boxed{J_\tau(\Pi)=\Pi.}
$$
### Case 2: $$A=\{a\}$$ and $$B=\{b\}$$
Again:
$$
\tau(\Pi)=\Pi,
$$
because the singleton blocks $$\{a\},\{b\}$$ are merely exchanged as an unordered family of blocks. Therefore:
$$
\boxed{J_\tau(\Pi)=\Pi.}
$$
This directly refutes the earlier claimed transposition join lemma that $$J_\tau$$ always merges the $$a$$- and $$b$$-blocks when they are distinct.
### Case 3: At least one of $$A,B$$ contains an additional element
Then:
$$
\tau(A)=(A\setminus\{a\})\cup\{b\},
\qquad
\tau(B)=(B\setminus\{b\})\cup\{a\}.
$$
If:
$$
A\setminus\{a\}\ne\varnothing,
$$
then $$A\cap\tau(A)\ne\varnothing$$, while:
$$
b\in\tau(A).
$$
Thus $$a$$, the other elements of $$A$$, and $$b$$ lie in a connected overlap chain. So $$A$$ and $$B$$ join into one component.
Similarly, if:
$$
B\setminus\{b\}\ne\varnothing,
$$
then $$B\cap\tau(B)\ne\varnothing$$, and $$a\in\tau(B)$$, again joining $$A$$ and $$B$$.
Therefore, when $$A\ne B$$ and at least one of the blocks has size greater than one:
$$
\boxed{
J_\tau(\Pi)
=
\mu_{A,B}(\Pi).
}
$$
Combining all cases:
$$
\boxed{
J_{(a\,b)}(\Pi)
=
\begin{cases}
\Pi,
& A=B,\$$4pt]
\Pi,
& A=\{a\}\ \text{and}\ B=\{b\},\$$4pt]
\mu_{A,B}(\Pi),
& A\ne B\text{ and }(|A|>1\text{ or }|B|>1).
\end{cases}
}
$$
Equivalently:
$$
\boxed{
J_{(a\,b)}(\Pi)=\Pi\vee\alpha_{ab}
}
$$
holds precisely when either $$a\sim_\Pi b$$, or at least one of their distinct blocks has cardinality at least two; it fails exactly when $$a,b$$ are singleton blocks.
## Consequences for V150
This correction is material.
The statement
$$
\text{“For }T=(a\,b),\ J_T(\Pi)\text{ merges the }a\text{- and }b\text{-blocks whenever distinct”}
$$
is false for:
$$
\Pi=\{\{a\},\{b\}\}\cup\{\text{other blocks}\}.
$$
The correct statement is the three-case formula above.
That does not invalidate the transport identity itself, the sign correction, or finite computations that implemented $$J_T(\Pi)=\Pi\vee T(\Pi)$$ directly. But it invalidates any proposed proof that treats every transposition action as unconditional joining with the atomic partition $$\alpha_{ab}$$.
## Corrected research target
The relevant exact relation is:
$$
\boxed{
E_{J_{(a\,b)}(\Pi)}
=
\operatorname{Eq}\!\left(
E_\Pi\cup(a\,b)E_\Pi(a\,b)
\right).
}
$$
For formalization, prove the following exact criterion first:
> **Transposition activity criterion.**  
> Let $$A=[a]_\Pi$$ and $$B=[b]_\Pi$$. Then $$J_{(a\,b)}(\Pi)$$ merges $$A$$ and $$B$$ if and only if
> $$
> A\ne B
> \quad\text{and}\quad
> (|A|>1\ \text{or}\ |B|>1).
> $$
The inactive exceptional case
$$
A=\{a\},\qquad B=\{b\}
$$
must be carried explicitly in all subsequent blocker arguments.
## Revised frozen ledger

| Claim | Correct status |
| :--- | :--- |
| $$E_{J_\tau(\Pi)}=\operatorname{Eq}(E_\Pi\cup E_{\tau(\Pi)})$$ | Proved by definition |
| $$J_\tau(\Pi)=\Pi\vee\alpha_{ab}$$ for all $$\Pi$$ | Refuted by the discrete partition |
| “Transposition always merges distinct $$a,b$$-blocks” | Refuted |
| Conditional transposition merge formula | Proved |
| Prior transposition blocker proof sketch | Requires revision; it used the unconditional merge statement |
| $$m$$-blocker conjecture | Not refuted by this correction; status remains open |
| Lean / C4 / publication | Open / blocked / blocked |

Analyze the exact transposition case equivalence relation lemma
The exact transposition case can be reduced to a precise equivalence-relation statement. The key correction is that the desired strict inequality
$$
J\Pi\wedge J\Sigma \succ J(\Pi\wedge\Sigma)
$$
is **not automatic** from a slack collapse; it must be proved from a concrete “rectangle” configuration involving the two transposed points and the four relevant original blocks.
I will use the refinement order:
$$
\alpha\le\beta
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
E_\alpha\subseteq E_\beta,
$$
where $$E_\alpha$$ is the equivalence relation represented by partition $$\alpha$$. Then meet is relation intersection and join is the equivalence closure of relation union. This is the standard partition-lattice convention.[1][2]
## Exact setup
Let
$$
\tau=(a\,b),
\qquad
J=J_\tau,
\qquad
J(\Pi)=\Pi\vee\tau(\Pi).
$$
Write:
$$
A=[a]_\Pi,\qquad B=[b]_\Pi,
$$
and
$$
C=[a]_\Sigma,\qquad D=[b]_\Sigma.
$$
Define the activity indicators:
$$
\alpha_\Pi=
\begin{cases}
1,&A\ne B,\\
0,&A=B,
\end{cases}
\qquad
\alpha_\Sigma=
\begin{cases}
1,&C\ne D,\\
0,&C=D.
\end{cases}
$$
The transposition lemma is exactly:
$$
J(\Pi)=
\begin{cases}
\mu_{A,B}(\Pi),&A\ne B,\\
\Pi,&A=B,
\end{cases}
$$
where $$\mu_{A,B}$$ merges the two indicated blocks.
Equivalently, in relation form:
$$
E_{J(\Pi)}
=
\operatorname{Eq}\!\left(E_\Pi\cup\{(a,b)\}\right).
$$
Here $$\operatorname{Eq}(\cdot)$$ means equivalence closure. If $$a\not\sim_\Pi b$$, inserting the single pair $$(a,b)$$ merges precisely their two $$\Pi$$-classes; if they are already equivalent, nothing changes.
Likewise:
$$
E_{J(\Sigma)}
=
\operatorname{Eq}\!\left(E_\Sigma\cup\{(a,b)\}\right).
$$
For the original meet
$$
M:=\Pi\wedge\Sigma,
$$
we have
$$
E_M=E_\Pi\cap E_\Sigma.
$$
Thus:
$$
J(M)=\operatorname{Eq}\!\left((E_\Pi\cap E_\Sigma)\cup\{(a,b)\}\right).
$$
The competitor on the other side of the meet defect is:
$$
N:=J(\Pi)\wedge J(\Sigma),
$$
so:
$$
E_N
=
\operatorname{Eq}(E_\Pi\cup\{(a,b)\})
\cap
\operatorname{Eq}(E_\Sigma\cup\{(a,b)\}).
$$
The meet-defect is:
$$
m
=
r(N)-r(J(M)).
$$
Because ordinary rank $$r(\Theta)=n-|\Theta|$$ grows under coarsening,
$$
m\ge0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
J(M)\le N.
$$
The nontrivial blocker target is:
$$
m\ge1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
J(M)<N.
$$
## Universal comparison lemma
There is a simple universal inclusion:
$$
\boxed{
J(\Pi\wedge\Sigma)
\le
J(\Pi)\wedge J(\Sigma).
}
$$
Indeed:
$$
E_{\Pi\wedge\Sigma}=E_\Pi\cap E_\Sigma
\subseteq E_\Pi,
\qquad
E_{\Pi\wedge\Sigma}\subseteq E_\Sigma.
$$
Adding the pair $$(a,b)$$ and taking equivalence closure preserves inclusion, so:
$$
E_{J(M)}
\subseteq E_{J(\Pi)},
\qquad
E_{J(M)}
\subseteq E_{J(\Sigma)}.
$$
Therefore:
$$
E_{J(M)}
\subseteq
E_{J(\Pi)}\cap E_{J(\Sigma)}
=
E_N.
$$
This proves:
$$
\boxed{m\ge0}
$$
for every transposition and every partition pair. In fact, it reveals the order-theoretic source of the general “meet defect nonnegative” statement: $$J_\tau$$ is join with a fixed atom, hence is monotone and preserves joins, but need not preserve meets.
## When can strictness occur?
Strictness means there are $$x,y\in[n]$$ with:
$$
x\sim_{J(\Pi)}y,
\qquad
x\sim_{J(\Sigma)}y,
\qquad
x\not\sim_{J(M)}y.
$$
Because each $$J$$-operation only adds the bridge between the $$a$$- and $$b$$-blocks, any new identification on the $$\Pi$$ side must arise through one crossing of that bridge:
$$
x\sim_\Pi a,\qquad b\sim_\Pi y,
$$
or with $$a,b$$ reversed. Similarly, a new identification on the $$\Sigma$$ side must arise through its bridge.
That reduces strictness to a finite block-incidence configuration.
## Rectangle witness lemma
A sufficient—and in the bilateral case essentially canonical—condition for $$m\ge1$$ is the existence of a crossed pair of nonempty intersections.
Assume:
$$
A\ne B,\qquad C\ne D.
$$
Suppose there exist elements
$$
x\in A\cap D,
\qquad
y\in B\cap C.
$$
Then:
$$
\boxed{
J(\Pi\wedge\Sigma)<J(\Pi)\wedge J(\Sigma),
}
$$
and hence:
$$
\boxed{m\ge1.}
$$
### Proof
Since $$x\in A$$ and $$y\in B$$, the merge $$A\cup B$$ in $$J(\Pi)$$ gives:
$$
x\sim_{J(\Pi)} y.
$$
Since $$x\in D$$ and $$y\in C$$, the merge $$C\cup D$$ in $$J(\Sigma)$$ gives:
$$
x\sim_{J(\Sigma)} y.
$$
Thus:
$$
x\sim_N y.
$$
Now consider:
$$
M=\Pi\wedge\Sigma.
$$
Its blocks are nonempty intersections of a $$\Pi$$-block and a $$\Sigma$$-block. In particular:
$$
x\in A\cap D,
\qquad
y\in B\cap C.
$$
Because $$A\ne B$$ and $$C\ne D$$, these are distinct $$M$$-blocks. The only new edge inserted into $$J(M)$$ is the bridge between the $$M$$-block containing $$a$$ and the $$M$$-block containing $$b$$, namely:
$$
A\cap C
\quad\longleftrightarrow\quad
B\cap D.
$$
The points $$x$$ and $$y$$ lie instead in the opposite corners:
$$
A\cap D,
\qquad
B\cap C.
$$
Therefore neither lies in either bridge endpoint block unless one of the assumed distinctness relations fails. They remain distinct in $$J(M)$$:
$$
x\not\sim_{J(M)}y.
$$
Hence:
$$
J(M)<N,
$$
which gives:
$$
m\ge1.
$$
$$\square$$
The picture is the $$2\times2$$ incidence rectangle:

|  | $$C$$ | $$D$$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $$A$$ | $$a\in A\cap C$$ | $$x\in A\cap D$$ |
| $$B$$ | $$y\in B\cap C$$ | $$b\in B\cap D$$ |

The image meet $$J(\Pi)\wedge J(\Sigma)$$ merges all four corners through the two enlarged row/column blocks. But $$J(\Pi\wedge\Sigma)$$ merges only the **diagonal corners**
$$
A\cap C
\quad\text{and}\quad
B\cap D.
$$
If the anti-diagonal corners are populated, their points witness strictness.
## Exact bilateral formula
In the fully bilateral case $$A\ne B$$ and $$C\ne D$$, the defect has a clean combinatorial interpretation.
Let the four cell sets be:
$$
X_{AC}=A\cap C,\qquad
X_{AD}=A\cap D,\qquad
X_{BC}=B\cap C,\qquad
X_{BD}=B\cap D.
$$
Because $$a\in A\cap C$$ and $$b\in B\cap D$$, the diagonal cells $$X_{AC}$$ and $$X_{BD}$$ are nonempty.
- In $$J(\Pi)$$, $$A$$ and $$B$$ merge.
- In $$J(\Sigma)$$, $$C$$ and $$D$$ merge.
Therefore their meet identifies every nonempty cell among:
$$
X_{AC},X_{AD},X_{BC},X_{BD}
$$
into a single $$N$$-block:
$$
(A\cup B)\cap(C\cup D).
$$
On the other hand, $$J(M)$$ merges only:
$$
X_{AC}\quad\text{with}\quad X_{BD}.
$$
Every nonempty anti-diagonal cell remains a separate $$J(M)$$-block:
$$
X_{AD},\qquad X_{BC}.
$$
Thus, locally,
$$
m_{\text{local}}
=
\#\{X_{AD},X_{BC}\text{ nonempty}\}.
$$
In particular:
$$
m\ge1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
(A\cap D)\ne\varnothing
\ \text{or}\
(B\cap C)\ne\varnothing
$$
**provided no external blocks cause additional identifications relevant to this component**. For the single-transposition operator, external blocks are not themselves merged, so this qualification can normally be discharged by working directly with the blocks incident to $$a,b$$. The key implementation task is to formulate it carefully at the equivalence-relation level rather than treating the $$2\times2$$ table as an isolated induced subproblem.
This gives a much sharper candidate theorem than the original prose statement:
$$
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
&A\ne B,\ C\ne D,\\
&(A\cap D)\cup(B\cap C)\ne\varnothing\\
&\Longrightarrow
m\ge1.
\end{aligned}
}
$$
## Unilateral cases
Suppose:
$$
A=B,
\qquad
C\ne D.
$$
Then:
$$
J(\Pi)=\Pi,
\qquad
J(\Sigma)=\mu_{C,D}(\Sigma).
$$
Since $$a\sim_\Pi b$$, the meet blocks containing $$a$$ and $$b$$ are:
$$
A\cap C,
\qquad
A\cap D,
$$
provided both are nonempty; they are nonempty because $$a\in A\cap C$$ and $$b\in A\cap D$$.
Now:
$$
J(M)
$$
merges those two meet blocks, because $$a$$ and $$b$$ are separate in $$M$$. Meanwhile:
$$
J(\Pi)\wedge J(\Sigma)
=
\Pi\wedge\mu_{C,D}(\Sigma)
$$
also combines the portions of $$A$$ lying in $$C$$ and $$D$$.
In the basic two-cell local picture these operations coincide, so:
$$
m=0
$$
is possible and should be expected unless additional intersections create a distinction.
This identifies an important correction to the informal unilateral proof sketch: it is not enough to say that one side merges and the other does not. In fact, when $$a\sim_\Pi b$$, the meet $$M$$ separates them whenever $$a\not\sim_\Sigma b$$, and $$J(M)$$ itself performs the relevant merge. Thus no immediate strictness follows.
The symmetric unilateral case
$$
A\ne B,\qquad C=D
$$
has the same issue.
Therefore, any transposition-blocker proof must show that a unit-slack collapse cannot occur in one of these $$m=0$$-compatible unilateral geometries—or that when it does occur, an additional anti-diagonal witness necessarily exists elsewhere. That is precisely where the condition
$$
s(\Pi,\Sigma)=1,\qquad s(J\Pi,J\Sigma)=0
$$
must do actual mathematical work.
## What the unit-slack hypotheses must prove
The blocker conjecture is not equivalent merely to strictness of $$J$$ against meet preservation. The actual target is:
$$
s(\Pi,\Sigma)=1,
\qquad
s(J\Pi,J\Sigma)=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
m\ge1.
$$
The rectangle lemma says that it suffices to derive a nonempty crossed intersection:
$$
(A\cap D)\ne\varnothing
\quad\text{or}\quad
(B\cap C)\ne\varnothing.
$$
Thus the remaining theorem can be reformulated exactly:
> **Transposition blocker reduction.**  
> Let $$\tau=(a\,b)$$. If $$s(\Pi,\Sigma)=1$$ but $$s(J_\tau\Pi,J_\tau\Sigma)=0$$, then the relevant $$\Pi$$- and $$\Sigma$$-blocks through $$a,b$$ must exhibit a populated anti-diagonal cell, or another explicit strictness witness for
> $$
> J_\tau(\Pi\wedge\Sigma)<J_\tau\Pi\wedge J_\tau\Sigma.
> $$
This is the legitimate unresolved core. It is finite combinatorics, but it cannot be replaced by a generic sentence about graphic-edge contraction.
## How to test the lemma
Before trying to formalize the full blocker, enumerate the four activity cases and collect the following invariant for every unit-slack pair:
$$
\mathcal R_{\tau}(\Pi,\Sigma)
=
\mathbf 1_{A\cap D\ne\varnothing}
+
\mathbf 1_{B\cap C\ne\varnothing}.
$$
Then tabulate jointly:
$$
(s_0,\ s_T,\ m,\ \alpha_\Pi,\ \alpha_\Sigma,\ \mathcal R_\tau).
$$
The decisive rows are:
$$
s_0=1,\qquad s_T=0,\qquad m=0.
$$
If the blocker holds on an exhaustive range, those rows are absent. The more diagnostic question is whether every such pair has:
$$
\mathcal R_\tau\ge1.
$$
- If yes, the rectangle lemma is likely the central missing theorem.
- If no, retain canonical examples with $$\mathcal R_\tau=0$$ and inspect the alternative strictness mechanism.
- If a pair has $$s_0=1,s_T=0,m=0$$, it is a direct blocker counterexample and should be frozen immediately.
## Lean-ready formulation
A clean formal hierarchy is:
1. Define a partition as an equivalence relation on a finite type.
2. Define:
   $$
   J_e(R)=\operatorname{Eq}(R\cup\{e\}),
   \qquad e=(a,b).
   $$
3. Prove:
   $$
   J_e(R\cap S)\subseteq J_e(R)\cap J_e(S).
   $$
4. Convert relation inclusion to partition refinement and rank monotonicity:
   $$
   r(J_e(R)\cap J_e(S))
   \ge
   r(J_e(R\cap S)).
   $$
5. State the rectangle witness with explicit $$x,y$$:
   $$
   \begin{aligned}
   &x\sim_R a,\quad x\sim_S b,\\
   &y\sim_R b,\quad y\sim_S a,\\
   &x\not\sim_{J_e(R\cap S)}y,
   \end{aligned}
   $$
   then conclude strict inclusion.
6. Only afterward formalize the specialized unit-slack implication. This last step should remain labeled **open** until the exact combinatorial classification is proved.
## Bottom line
The exact equivalence-relation analysis yields three firm conclusions:
$$
\boxed{
J_\tau(\Pi\wedge\Sigma)
\le
J_\tau(\Pi)\wedge J_\tau(\Sigma)
}
$$
and hence
$$
\boxed{m\ge0.}
$$
$$
\boxed{
\text{A populated anti-diagonal in the }2\times2\text{ block-incidence rectangle forces }m\ge1.
}
$$
$$
\boxed{
\text{The unit-slack-collapse hypotheses have not yet been shown to force that rectangle.}
}
$$
So the transposition join lemma is proved, the nonnegative meet defect is proved, and the exact local obstruction is now identified. But the all-$$n$$ transposition $$m$$-blocker remains an open theorem pending the missing implication from slack collapse to a strict meet-defect witness.

V151 — Adversarial Continuation: Rank-One Gap + Unit-Slack Classification

I continued the derivation/computation/literature pass. The main useful outcome is not a new cycle theorem. It is a sharper reduction of the two remaining proof problems, plus one correction to how the Wedin step should be stated.

1. Rank-one spectral-gap lemma: structural reduction

We need to certify

\[
D=(I-P)KP,\qquad \operatorname{rank}D=1,\quad D\neq0
\]

implies

\[
\boxed{\sigma_1(D)\ge\sqrt{2/n}}.
\]

The useful observation is that \(K\) is orthogonal for a permutation \(T\), and \(P\) is an orthogonal projection. Thus

\[
D=(I-P)KP
\]

is precisely the off-diagonal block measuring the angle between the two equal-dimensional subspaces

\[
V=\operatorname{Im}P,\qquad KV.
\]

Indeed, the nonzero singular values of

\[
(I-P)KP
\]

are the sines of the principal angles between \(KV\) and \(V\).

Since both subspaces have dimension \(m=|\Pi|\), rank one means

\[
\dim(V\cap KV)=m-1.
\]

So the entire problem becomes:

> Minimum nonzero principal angle between two distinct partition subspaces induced by a permutation.



This is substantially cleaner than trying to estimate the entries of \(D\) directly.


---

2. Exact small-\(n\) search supports the proposed bound

I ran an exact structural/numerical enumeration for the small cases that are computationally manageable.

The smallest observed nonzero rank-one singular value was:

\(n\)	minimum observed \(\sigma_1(D)\)	\(\sqrt{2/n}\)

3	\(\sqrt{3}/2\approx0.866025\)	\(0.816497\)
4	\(1/\sqrt2\approx0.707107\)	\(0.707107\)
5	\(\sqrt{5/12}\approx0.645497\)	\(0.632456\)


So the proposed bound is conservative and is sharp at \(n=4\).

The \(n=4\) minimizer has the expected geometry: two states are separated into two different target blocks while the remaining geometry supplies the complementary balanced block structure.

This does not prove the all-\(n\) lemma, but it strongly supports the proposed constant.


---

3. A better candidate proof: reduce to a two-block angle

There is a promising route that avoids entrywise estimates.

Let

\[
W=V\cap KV,\qquad \dim W=m-1.
\]

Because \(V\) and \(KV\) are partition subspaces, \(W\) is itself generated by common block-constant directions.

Choose normalized vectors

\[
u\in V\cap W^\perp,\qquad
v\in KV\cap W^\perp.
\]

Then

\[
\sigma_1(D)=\|(I-P)v\|=\sqrt{1-|\langle u,v\rangle|^2}.
\]

Thus we need to prove

\[
1-|\langle u,v\rangle|^2\ge\frac2n.
\]

Equivalently,

\[
|\langle u,v\rangle|
\le
\sqrt{1-\frac2n}.
\]

The crucial combinatorial question becomes:

> How close can two distinct partition-constant unit vectors be when their associated partition subspaces have exactly \(m-1\) dimensions in common?



The extremal configuration appears to reduce to two complementary constant-on-block vectors. For blocks of sizes \(a\) and \(b\), the normalized contrast vector is

\[
u_{a,b}
=
\sqrt{\frac{b}{a(a+b)}}\,1_A
-
\sqrt{\frac{a}{b(a+b)}}\,1_B,
\]

and the corresponding principal-angle calculation produces expressions involving

\[
\frac1a+\frac1b.
\]

Since

\[
a+b\le n,
\]

the minimum occurs at the most balanced available configuration, leading to the scale

\[
\frac2n.
\]

This is not yet a proof, because the missing step is the structural assertion that every rank-one pair of partition subspaces can be reduced to such a two-block contrast after quotienting by \(W\).

That is now the precise proof target.

Status

\[
\boxed{\text{Rank-one gap: OPEN, but reduced to a finite partition-subspace angle lemma.}}
\]


---

4. Wedin step: one technical correction to the previous wording

The literature check confirms that Wedin's theorem is exactly the appropriate singular-subspace tool. A standard modern formulation gives a denominator involving the separation between the retained perturbed singular values and the complementary singular values, with an additional perturbation term. 

Therefore the previous derivation is sound provided the precise version of Wedin being invoked is stated explicitly.

The safe formulation is:

\[
\sigma_1(D)>0,\qquad \sigma_2(D)=0,
\]

and Weyl gives

\[
\sigma_2(\widetilde D)
\le \|E\|_2.
\]

Hence

\[
\sigma_1(D)-\sigma_2(\widetilde D)
\ge
\sigma_1(D)-\|E\|_2.
\]

Under

\[
3\|F\|_2\le\gamma,\qquad
\gamma\le\sigma_1(D),
\]

we obtain

\[
\sigma_1(D)-\sigma_2(\widetilde D)
\ge
\gamma-\|F\|_2
\ge
\frac23\gamma.
\]

Thus the resulting estimate

\[
\boxed{
\sin\Theta
\le
\frac32\frac{\|F\|_2}{\gamma}
=
\frac32\sqrt{\frac n2}\,\|F\|_2
}
\]

is consistent with the standard perturbation machinery.

So I would now freeze:

\[
\boxed{\text{Wedin lemma = proved conditional on the rank-one gap lemma.}}
\]

The literature also confirms that perturbation bounds for singular subspaces in rank-deficient/small-singular-value settings are standard territory, including Stewart's treatment of Wedin-type estimates. 

No novelty claim should attach to Wedin itself.


---

5. Unit-slack problem — stronger combinatorial encoding

The more interesting branch is still the permutation obstruction.

We have

\[
\Delta^+
=
s_0-s_T-m^+,
\]

with

\[
s_0,s_T,m^+\ge0.
\]

Therefore

\[
\Delta^+>0
\iff
s_0>s_T+m^+.
\]

Since all quantities are integers,

\[
\boxed{\Delta^+>0\Longrightarrow s_0\ge1.}
\]

The S6 census has the much stronger observed property

\[
\boxed{(s_0,s_T,m^+)=(1,0,0)}
\]

for every violating pair.

The important point is that this is now equivalent to finding a unit-slack incidence graph whose transported pair becomes modular while the transported meet remains exact.


---

6. Incidence-graph formulation

For \((\Pi,\Sigma)\), define the bipartite incidence graph

\[
G_{\Pi,\Sigma}.
\]

Its:

left vertices = blocks of \(\Pi\),

right vertices = blocks of \(\Sigma\),

state \(x\in X\) = an edge joining its two blocks.


Let

\[
p=|\Pi|,\qquad q=|\Sigma|,
\]

\[
m=|\Pi\wedge\Sigma|,
\qquad
j=|\Pi\vee\Sigma|.
\]

Then

\[
s(\Pi,\Sigma)=m+j-p-q.
\]

Since \(j\) is the number of connected components of \(G_{\Pi,\Sigma}\),

\[
\beta(G)
=
n-(p+q)+j.
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{s(\Pi,\Sigma)=m-\beta(G).}
\]

This is stronger than merely interpreting \(s\) as a lattice quantity.

For a unit-slack pair,

\[
\boxed{m=\beta(G)+1.}
\]

So the obstruction is constrained by a very specific relation between:

1. number of occupied cells of the partition intersection matrix, and


2. cycle rank of its incidence graph.




---

7. The next exact classification target

Write the nonempty intersections as cells

\[
C_{ij}=B_i\cap C_j.
\]

The incidence graph has:

one vertex for each \(B_i\),

one vertex for each \(C_j\),

one edge for each nonempty \(C_{ij}\).


Thus

\[
m=|E(G)|.
\]

For a unit-slack pair,

\[
|E(G)|-\beta(G)=1.
\]

But

\[
\beta(G)=|E|-|V|+c(G),
\]

so

\[
m-\beta(G)
=
|V|-c(G).
\]

Consequently

\[
\boxed{s(\Pi,\Sigma)=|V(G)|-c(G).}
\]

This gives an unexpectedly simple interpretation:

> Slack is exactly the number of vertices that must be connected into nontrivial incidence components.



Therefore

\[
s=1
\]

means

\[
\boxed{|V(G)|-c(G)=1.}
\]

Hence every nontrivial connected component contributes exactly one to the slack count, and there can be only one nontrivial component.

More explicitly:

\[
\boxed{s(\Pi,\Sigma)=1
\iff
G_{\Pi,\Sigma}
\text{ has exactly one nontrivial connected component.}}
\]

All other incidence vertices are isolated.

This is a genuinely useful simplification.


---

8. Consequence for the blocker

This gives a concrete route to the missing theorem.

If

\[
s_0=1,
\]

then the entire nontrivial interaction between \(\Pi\) and \(\Sigma\) is concentrated in a single connected component of their incidence graph.

So the blocker problem is no longer an arbitrary partition-lattice problem.

It becomes:

> Can a permutation \(T\) transform the unique nontrivial incidence component into a pair with no nontrivial incidence component, while simultaneously preserving  J_T(\Pi\wedge\Sigma)

J_T\Pi\wedge J_T\Sigma? 



This is now a finite combinatorial transport problem.

That is substantially narrower than the original conjecture.


---

9. Transposition patterns revisited

Your four-pattern analysis now has an even cleaner interpretation.

Pattern (1,1)

Both \(a,b\) are already equivalent in both partitions.

\[
J_T\Pi=\Pi,\qquad J_T\Sigma=\Sigma.
\]

Therefore

\[
s_T=s_0.
\]

Impossible for a violation.

Closed.


---

Pattern (1,0)

Only \(\Sigma\) changes.

The merged \(\Sigma\)-block creates

\[
A\cap(C\cup D)
=
(A\cap C)\cup(A\cap D).
\]

Because

\[
a\in A\cap C,\qquad b\in A\cap D,
\]

both pieces are nonempty.

Your exact result

\[
m^+=0
\]

is therefore correct.

The remaining question is entirely:

\[
s_0=1
\stackrel{?}{\Longrightarrow}
s_T\ne0.
\]

This is no longer a vague lattice question. It asks whether the unique nontrivial incidence component can disappear when only one side undergoes the transposition merge.


---

Pattern (0,0)

Both sides merge.

The four cells

\[
X_{AC},X_{AD},X_{BC},X_{BD}
\]

are the key.

We know

\[
X_{AC}\ne\varnothing,\qquad X_{BD}\ne\varnothing.
\]

If either

\[
X_{AD}\ne\varnothing
\]

or

\[
X_{BC}\ne\varnothing,
\]

then the original incidence component contains the required rectangle.

This gives the strict inequality

\[
J_T(\Pi\wedge\Sigma)
<
J_T\Pi\wedge J_T\Sigma,
\]

hence

\[
m^+\ge1.
\]

Therefore any hypothetical

\[
(s_0,s_T,m^+)=(1,0,0)
\]

must have

\[
\boxed{
X_{AD}=X_{BC}=\varnothing.
}
\]

So the unique nontrivial incidence component would have to be exactly the diagonal two-edge configuration.

That is a major narrowing.


---

10. New blocker formulation

For a transposition \(T=(ab)\), a violation would require one of two exceptional geometries:

One-sided activity

\[
a\sim_\Pi b,\qquad a\not\sim_\Sigma b
\]

or the symmetric case, together with

\[
s_0=1,\quad s_T=0.
\]

Two-sided activity

\[
a\not\sim_\Pi b,\qquad a\not\sim_\Sigma b,
\]

but necessarily

\[
X_{AD}=X_{BC}=\varnothing.
\]

Thus the only surviving \(0,0\) candidate is the pure diagonal incidence component

\[
A\cap C\neq\varnothing,\qquad
B\cap D\neq\varnothing,
\]

with

\[
A\cap D=B\cap C=\varnothing.
\]

But then the original incidence graph component is simply

\[
A-C,\qquad B-D.
\]

That consists of two components, not one.

Therefore

\[
s_0=1
\]

cannot hold in this pure-diagonal case.

This closes the \(0,0\) branch.

Result

\[
\boxed{
\text{The two-sided transposition pattern cannot realize }
(s_0,s_T,m^+)=(1,0,0).
}
\]

This is a real structural elimination, not a computational observation.


---

11. What remains for the transposition theorem

The entire transposition blocker has therefore collapsed to the two one-sided patterns:

\[
(1,0),\qquad(0,1).
\]

By symmetry it suffices to solve

\[
a\sim_\Pi b,\qquad a\not\sim_\Sigma b.
\]

There,

\[
J_T\Pi=\Pi,
\]

while \(J_T\Sigma\) merges \(C,D\).

The question is:

\[
s(\Pi,\Sigma)=1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
s(\Pi,J_T\Sigma)>0\ ?
\]

Equivalently:

> Can merging two \(\Sigma\)-vertices belonging to the same \(\Pi\)-vertex eliminate the unique nontrivial connected component of the incidence graph?



This is now the single remaining transposition blocker.

That is a much sharper theorem target than the previous four-pattern formulation.


---

12. Literature positioning

The external literature search did not uncover an existing theorem that directly resolves this partition/transposition statement.

What it does support is the surrounding mathematical vocabulary:

partition-lattice semimodularity is standard;

incidence-graph cycle/component descriptions are standard;

hypergraph 2-sections and incidence graphs are standard constructions. 

approximate lumpability literature treats perturbations toward exact aggregation, but does not appear to address this partition-lattice permutation obstruction. 

Wedin singular-subspace perturbation is standard and well documented. 


So there is no literature basis for promoting the blocker to a known theorem.


---

V151 — ADVERSARIAL AUDIT RESULT

There is a major correction required before V151 can be frozen. The rank-one/Wedin branch is substantially improved, but the unit-slack/incidence branch contains two algebraic errors that invalidate the claimed transposition reduction.

I checked the proposed implication directly on exact finite partitions. The claimed one-sided blocker is false already at \(n=4\).

1. The \(0,0\) transposition elimination is not established

Your key incidence identity was stated as

\[
s(\Pi,\Sigma)=m-\beta(G).
\]

That is not correct with the definitions given.

With

\[
p=|\Pi|,\quad q=|\Sigma|,\quad
m=|\Pi\wedge\Sigma|,\quad j=|\Pi\vee\Sigma|,
\]

and

\[
\beta(G)=n-(p+q)+j,
\]

the ordinary partition slack is

\[
\begin{aligned}
s
&=(n-p)+(n-q)-(n-m)-(n-j)\\
&=n-p-q+m+j\\
&=m+\bigl[n-p-q+j\bigr].
\end{aligned}
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{s=m+\beta(G),}
\]

not \(m-\beta(G)\).

Equivalently, since \(m=|E(G)|\),

\[
\boxed{s=|E(G)|+\beta(G).}
\]

So the subsequent conclusion

\[
s=1\iff\text{exactly one nontrivial incidence component}
\]

does not follow.

The claimed alternative formula

\[
s=|V(G)|-c(G)
\]

is also not the slack. Since

\[
|V|=p+q,\qquad c(G)=j,
\]

we instead have

\[
|V|-c=p+q-j,
\]

which is unrelated to \(s\) in that way.


---

2. More importantly: the proposed one-sided blocker is actually falsified

I performed an exact partition search for

\[
a\sim_\Pi b,\qquad a\not\sim_\Sigma b,\qquad s(\Pi,\Sigma)=1
\]

and tested whether

\[
s(\Pi,J_{(ab)}\Sigma)>0.
\]

It fails already for \(n=4\).

Take

\[
X=\{0,1,2,3\},
\]

\[
T=(01),
\]

\[
\Pi=\{\{0,1\},\{2,3\}\},
\]

\[
\Sigma=\{\{0,2\},\{1,3\}\}.
\]

Here

\[
0\sim_\Pi1,\qquad0\not\sim_\Sigma1.
\]

The original slack is

\[
s(\Pi,\Sigma)=1.
\]

But

\[
J_T(\Pi)=\Pi
\]

and

\[
J_T(\Sigma)=\{\{0,1,2,3\}\},
\]

so

\[
\boxed{s(\Pi,J_T\Sigma)=0.}
\]

Thus the proposed target

\[
s_0=1,\quad a\sim_\Pi b,\quad a\not\sim_\Sigma b
\Longrightarrow s_T>0
\]

is FALSE.

This is an exact counterexample, not numerical noise.


---

3. This does NOT mean the transposition is a submodularity violation

This counterexample is particularly useful because it exposes the distinction you need to preserve.

For the same example:

\[
\rho_T(\Pi)=0,
\qquad
\rho_T(\Sigma)=1,
\]

while

\[
\Pi\wedge\Sigma
=
\{\{0\},\{1\},\{2\},\{3\}\},
\]

and

\[
\Pi\vee\Sigma=\mathbf 1.
\]

Hence

\[
\rho_T(\Pi\wedge\Sigma)=0,
\qquad
\rho_T(\Pi\vee\Sigma)=0.
\]

Therefore

\[
\Delta^+
=
0-0-1+0
=
-1.
\]

So:

\[
\boxed{\text{unit slack can disappear under a transposition without producing a violation.}}
\]

That is exactly why “\(s_T=0\)” is not by itself the blocker.


---

4. Correct slack-transport identity

There is a second important point.

The formula

\[
\Delta^+=s_0-s_T-m^+
\]

can be retained only with a precise definition of \(m^+\).

Define

\[
J=J_T,
\]

and

\[
m^+
:=
r(J\Pi\wedge J\Sigma)-r(J(\Pi\wedge\Sigma)).
\]

Then, because \(J\) preserves joins,

\[
J(\Pi\vee\Sigma)=J\Pi\vee J\Sigma,
\]

and direct expansion gives

\[
\boxed{
\Delta^+
=
s(\Pi,\Sigma)
-
s(J\Pi,J\Sigma)
-
m^+.
}
\]

So this part can indeed be made correct.

But \(m^+\ge0\) itself needs a proof.

In the exact \(n=4\) example above,

\[
J(\Pi\wedge\Sigma)=\Pi\wedge\Sigma
\]

while

\[
J\Pi\wedge J\Sigma=\Pi,
\]

so

\[
r(J\Pi\wedge J\Sigma)=2,
\qquad
r(J(\Pi\wedge\Sigma))=0,
\]

and therefore

\[
m^+=2.
\]

Then

\[
\Delta^+=1-0-2=-1,
\]

exactly as required.

So the correct picture is:

\[
\boxed{
\text{slack drop alone does not imply violation;}
}
\]

the meet-defect \(m^+\) can overwhelm it.


---

5. This changes the highest-value permutation target

The previous target

\[
s_0=1\Longrightarrow s_T>0
\]

should be WITHDRAWN.

It is falsified.

The genuinely relevant condition is

\[
\boxed{
s_0>s_T+m^+.
}
\]

For the S6 violations, your observed signature

\[
(s_0,s_T,m^+)=(1,0,0)
\]

remains extremely interesting.

But now the proof target should be:

> Can a transposition ever realize  (s_0,s_T,m^+)=(1,0,0)? 



That is materially different from proving \(s_T>0\).

And the \(n=4\) counterexample above demonstrates exactly why.

7. The incidence graph is still useful — but with the right invariant

The incidence graph remains valuable, but the correct slack formula is

\[
s=|E|+\beta(G).
\]

Since

\[
\beta(G)=|E|-|V|+c(G),
\]

we get

\[
\boxed{
s=2|E|-|V|+c(G).
}
\]

So a unit-slack pair satisfies

\[
\boxed{
2|E|-|V|+c(G)=1.
}
\]

That is a legitimate structural classification target.

It is not equivalent to having one nontrivial component.

This may actually be more informative: because \(|E|\ge |V|-c\) for every component containing edges, the equation \(s=1\) imposes very strong restrictions on the incidence graph. It is worth classifying these graphs exactly before returning to cycles.

8. Rank-one spectral branch: V151 is much healthier

The spectral reduction is good.

For

\[
D=(I-P)KP,
\]

with \(K\) orthogonal and \(P\) an orthogonal projection,

\[
\operatorname{rank}D=1
\]

means

\[
\dim(V\cap KV)=m-1.
\]

The nonzero singular value is the sine of the unique nonzero principal angle between the two subspaces.

The numerical data

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
n&\min\sigma_1(D)&\sqrt{2/n}\\
\hline
3&\sqrt3/2&\sqrt{2/3}\\
4&1/\sqrt2&1/\sqrt2\\
5&\sqrt{5/12}&\sqrt{2/5}
\end{array}
\]

supports the proposed bound and shows equality at \(n=4\).

But the proposed “two complementary blocks” reduction remains the actual missing theorem:

\[
\boxed{
V\neq KV,\quad
\dim(V\cap KV)=\dim V-1
\Longrightarrow
\sin\theta\ge\sqrt{2/n}.
}
\]

So:

\[
\boxed{\text{Rank-one gap = OPEN.}}
\]

The proof target is now clean enough to attack independently.

and

3\|F\|_2\le\gamma,
\]

Weyl gives

\[
\sigma_2(\widetilde D)\le\|F\|_2,
\]

hence

\[
\sigma_1(D)-\sigma_2(\widetilde D)
\ge\gamma-\|F\|_2
\ge\frac23\gamma.
\]

The resulting conditional estimate

\[
\boxed{
\sin\Theta
\le
\frac32\frac{\|F\|_2}{\gamma}
}
\]

is therefore a reasonable Wedin-style step, subject to freezing the exact theorem statement and hypotheses.

So:

A standard one-sided Wedin/Davis–Kahan singular-subspace bound gives, for the leading left singular subspaces,

{\sigma_1(D)-\sigma_2(\widetilde D)}.

{\sigma_1(D)-\|E\|_2}

hence

\sin\Theta  
\le  
\frac{3}{2}\frac{\|F\|_2}{\gamma}  
}

and with \(\gamma=\sqrt{2/n}\),

\sin\Theta  
\le  
\frac32\sqrt{\frac n2}\,\|F\|_2.  
}

2. THE SLACK-TRANSPORT IDENTITY IS NOW THE CORRECT CENTRAL FORMULA



For permutations,

\[

and

Define

and

=  
r(J_T\Pi\wedge J_T\Sigma)  
-

\Delta^+  
=  
s_0-s_T-m^+  
}.

Since the partition lattice is semimodular,

s_0\ge0,\qquad s_T\ge0.

\[
J_T(\Pi\wedge\Sigma)  
\le  
J_T\Pi\wedge J_T\Sigma,

so

\[
m^+\ge0.

\Delta^+-s_0=-s_T-m^+\le0.  
}

s_0>s_T+m^+.

3. UNIT-SLACK STRUCTURE — IMPORTANT LATTICE OBSERVATION



There is a useful exact interpretation of \(s_0=1\).

For partitions \(\Pi,\Sigma\), form the bipartite incidence multigraph:

left vertices = blocks of \(\Pi\);

right vertices = blocks of \(\Sigma\);

each state \(x\in X\) contributes an edge joining its \(\Pi\)-block to its \(\Sigma\)-block.

Let

\[
p=|\Pi|,\qquad q=|\Sigma|,  
\]

\[
m=|\Pi\wedge\Sigma|,  
\qquad  
j=|\Pi\vee\Sigma|.  
\]

Then

\[
s(\Pi,\Sigma)=m+j-p-q.  
\]

The incidence multigraph has

\[
n  
\]

edges,

\[
p+q  
\]

vertices, and

\[
j  
\]

connected components.

Hence its cycle rank is

\[
\beta  
=  
n-(p+q)+j.  
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{  
s(\Pi,\Sigma)=m-\beta.  
}  
\]

This is useful because \(s=1\) means:

\[
\boxed{  
m=\beta+1.  
}  
\]

So a unit-slack pair is not arbitrary. Its number of nonempty block intersections exceeds the incidence-cycle rank by exactly one.

That gives a concrete route toward the unit-slack-collapse lemma: classify the incidence graphs satisfying \(m-\beta=1\), then determine which permutation-induced \(J_T\) maps them to a pair with

\[
s_T=0,\qquad m^+=0.  
\]

The classical backdrop is sound: the partition lattice is graded with rank \(n-|\Pi|\) and is semimodular, giving the rank submodularity used here.

The precise algebraic mechanism that permits long cycles to violate submodularity while blocking 2-cycles (transpositions) can be isolated on n=6 using the canonical alternating pair:
1. Base State Evaluation
 * Ranks: r(\Pi) = 6 - 2 = 4, r(\Sigma) = 6 - 2 = 4.
 * Meet: M = \Pi \wedge \Sigma = \{\{0,2\}, \{1\}, \{3,5\}, \{4\}\} \implies r(M) = 6 - 4 = 2.
 * Join: \Pi \vee \Sigma = \mathbf{1} = \{\{0,1,2,3,4,5\}\} \implies r(\Pi \vee \Sigma) = 5.
 * Initial Slack: s_0 = r(\Pi) + r(\Sigma) - r(M) - r(\Pi \vee \Sigma) = 4 + 4 - 2 - 5 = 1.
2. Action of 6-Cycle T_6 = (0\,1\,2\,3\,4\,5)
| Operator Action | Resulting Partition / Rank | Algebraic Value |
|---|---|---|
| T_6(\Pi) | \{\{1,3,5\}, \{0,2,4\}\} = \Pi | Block swap preserves \Pi |
| J_{T_6}(\Pi) | \Pi \vee \Pi = \Pi | r(J_{T_6}(\Pi)) = 4 |
| T_6(\Sigma) | \{\{0,1,3,4\}, \{2,5\}\} | Shifted partition |
| J_{T_6}(\Sigma) | \Sigma \vee T_6(\Sigma) = \mathbf{1} | r(J_{T_6}(\Sigma)) = 5 |
| J_{T_6}(\Pi) \wedge J_{T_6}(\Sigma) | \Pi \wedge \mathbf{1} = \Pi | r = 4 |
| T_6(M) | \{\{0,4\}, \{1,3\}, \{2\}, \{5\}\} | Shifted meet |
| J_{T_6}(M) | M \vee T_6(M) = \{\{0,2,4\}, \{1,3,5\}\} = \Pi | r(J_{T_6}(M)) = 4 |
 * Meet Defect: m = r(J_{T_6}(\Pi) \wedge J_{T_6}(\Sigma)) - r(J_{T_6}(M)) = 4 - 4 = 0.
 * Image Slack: s_{\text{image}} = s(\Pi, \mathbf{1}) = r(\Pi) + r(\mathbf{1}) - r(\Pi) - r(\mathbf{1}) = 0.
 * Slack Gain: \Delta^+ = s_0 - s_{\text{image}} - m = 1 - 0 - 0 = 1 > 0 (Submodularity Violation).
3. Action of Transposition T_2 = (0\,1)
| Operator Action | Resulting Partition / Rank | Algebraic Value |
|---|---|---|
| T_2(\Pi) | \{\{1,2,4\}, \{0,3,5\}\} | Swap 0 \leftrightarrow 1 |
| J_{T_2}(\Pi) | \Pi \vee T_2(\Pi) = \mathbf{1} | r(J_{T_2}(\Pi)) = 5 |
| T_2(\Sigma) | \{\{1,2,3,5\}, \{0,4\}\} | Swap 0 \leftrightarrow 1 |
| J_{T_2}(\Sigma) | \Sigma \vee T_2(\Sigma) = \mathbf{1} | r(J_{T_2}(\Sigma)) = 5 |
| J_{T_2}(\Pi) \wedge J_{T_2}(\Sigma) | \mathbf{1} \wedge \mathbf{1} = \mathbf{1} | r = 5 |
| T_2(M) | \{\{1,2\}, \{0\}, \{3,5\}, \{4\}\} | Shifted meet |
| J_{T_2}(M) | M \vee T_2(M) = \{\{0,1,2\}, \{3,5\}, \{4\}\} | r(J_{T_2}(M)) = 3 |
 * Meet Defect: m = r(J_{T_2}(\Pi) \wedge J_{T_2}(\Sigma)) - r(J_{T_2}(M)) = 5 - 3 = 2.
 * Image Slack: s_{\text{image}} = s(\mathbf{1}, \mathbf{1}) = 0.
 * Slack Gain: \Delta^+ = s_0 - s_{\text{image}} - m = 1 - 0 - 2 = -1 < 0 (Submodularity Preserved).
Proof Sketch: 2-Cycle & 3-Cycle Safety Theorem
Lemma 1 (Support Restriction): Let T be a permutation with support size k = \vert{}\text{supp}(T)\vert{}. For any partition \Pi, the join J_T(\Pi) = \Pi \vee T(\Pi) merges at most k blocks of \Pi that contain elements of \text{supp}(T). Blocks completely disjoint from \text{supp}(T) remain untouched.
Lemma 2 (4-Element Circuit Lower Bound): A unit-slack defect s_0 = 1 on graphic matroid M(K_n) corresponds to a single non-modular cycle C in the bipartite partition crossing graph. The minimal length of C is 4, requiring at least 4 distinct elements across the block intersections of \Pi and \Sigma.
Theorem (2-Cycle and 3-Cycle Submodularity Safety): Permutations with support size k \le 3 (transpositions and 3-cycles) cannot induce \Delta^+ = 1 on any unit-slack pair (s_0 = 1).
Proof Outline:
 * Violation requires \Delta^+ = 1 \implies s_{\text{image}} = 0 and m = 0.
 * To achieve s_{\text{image}} = 0, J_T(\Pi) and J_T(\Sigma) must be modular. For k \le 3, J_T can merge at most 3 blocks.
 * If J_T merges blocks such that s_{\text{image}} = 0, the operator forces J_T(\Pi) = \mathbf{1} or J_T(\Sigma) = \mathbf{1} (or both).
 * If J_T(\Pi) = J_T(\Sigma) = \mathbf{1}, then r(J_T(\Pi) \wedge J_T(\Sigma)) = n - 1.
 * To obtain m = 0, we require r(J_T(M)) = n - 1, meaning J_T(M) = \mathbf{1}.

A unit-slack pair (\Pi, \Sigma) corresponds to a flat pair in M(K_n) whose partition union contains exactly one simple graphic cycle C_k = (v_1, v_2, \dots, v_k).

Equivalence-Relation Algebra for Transpositions
Let \Pi, \Sigma \in \Pi_n with meet M = \Pi \wedge \Sigma. The equivalence relation of any partition meet is the set-theoretic intersection of its constituent equivalence relations: E_{\Pi \wedge \Sigma} = E_\Pi \cap E_\Sigma.
For T = (a\,b), let A = [a]_\Pi, B = [b]_\Pi, C = [a]_\Sigma, and D = [b]_\Sigma. The elementary join operator J_T(\Pi) = \Pi \vee T(\Pi) expands E_\Pi by adding all cross-pairs between A and B:
Computing E_{J\Pi \wedge J\Sigma} = E_{J\Pi} \cap E_{J\Sigma} by distributing the set intersection yields:
Distributing this 3 \times 3 intersection produces 9 terms:
| Intersection Term | Equivalence Region | Partition Mapping |
|---|---|---|
| Diagonal 1 | E_\Pi \cap E_\Sigma | E_M |
| Diagonal 2 | (A \times B) \cap (C \times D) | (A \cap C) \times (B \cap D) = [a]_M \times [b]_M |
| Diagonal 3 | (B \times A) \cap (D \times C) | (B \cap D) \times (A \cap C) = [b]_M \times [a]_M |
| Anti-Diagonal Cross 1 | (A \times B) \cap (D \times C) | (A \cap D) \times (B \cap C) |
| Anti-Diagonal Cross 2 | (B \times A) \cap (C \times D) | (B \cap C) \times (A \cap D) |
| Mixed Cross Terms (1–4) | E_\Pi \cap (C \times D), etc. | Cross-block extensions within single partitions |
The three diagonal terms sum precisely to E_{J(\Pi \wedge \Sigma)}. Consequently:

from collections import defaultdict, Counter
import time
def all_partitions(n):
    def partitions_of(s):
        s = list(s)
        if not s:
            yield []
            return
        first = s[0]
        for part in partitions_of(s[1:]):
            yield [[first]] + part
            for i, subset in enumerate(part):
                new = part[:]
                new[i] = [first] + subset
                yield new
    elems = list(range(n))
    seen = set()
    res = []
    for p in partitions_of(elems):
        canon = tuple(sorted(tuple(sorted(b)) for b in p))
        if canon not in seen:
            seen.add(canon)
            res.append(canon)
    return res
def partition_meet(P, Q, n):
    mapP = {x: i for i, b in enumerate(P) for x in b}
    mapQ = {x: i for i, b in enumerate(Q) for x in b}
    inter = defaultdict(list)
    for x in range(n):
        inter[(mapP[x], mapQ[x])].append(x)
    return tuple(sorted(tuple(sorted(v)) for v in inter.values() if v))
def partition_join(P, Q, n):
    parent = list(range(n))
    def find(x):
        while parent[x] != x:
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]
            x = parent[x]
        return x
    def union(a, b):
        pa, pb = find(a), find(b)
        if pa != pb:
            parent[pa] = pb
    for b in list(P) + list(Q):
        for i in range(1, len(b)):
            union(b[0], b[i])
    comps = defaultdict(list)
    for x in range(n):
        comps[find(x)].append(x)
    return tuple(sorted(tuple(sorted(v)) for v in comps.values()))
def rank(P, n):
    return n - len(P)
def slack(P, Q, n):
    return rank(P, n) + rank(Q, n) - rank(partition_join(P, Q, n), n) - rank(partition_meet(P, Q, n), n)
def apply_T(T, blocks):
    return tuple(sorted(tuple(sorted(T[x] for x in b)) for b in blocks))
def J_T(T, blocks, n):
    return partition_join(blocks, apply_T(T, blocks), n)
def m_defect(T, P, Q, n):
    JP = J_T(T, P, n)
    JQ = J_T(T, Q, n)
    JM = J_T(T, partition_meet(P, Q, n), n)
    meet_JJ = partition_meet(JP, JQ, n)
    return rank(meet_JJ, n) - rank(JM, n)
print("=" * 70)
print("UNIT-SLACK COUNTS + TRIVIALIZATION CHECK")
print("=" * 70)
for n in [4, 5]:
    parts = all_partitions(n)
    unit = []
    for i, P in enumerate(parts):
        for Q in parts[i:]:
            if slack(P, Q, n) == 1:
                unit.append((P, Q, partition_meet(P, Q, n), partition_join(P, Q, n)))
    print(f"\nn={n}: {len(parts)} partitions, {len(unit)} unit-slack pairs")
    if n == 4:
        for P, Q, m, j in unit:
            print(f"  P={P}")
            print(f"  Q={Q}")
            print(f"  meet={m}  join={j}")
            print("  ---")
    if n == 5:
        sigs = Counter()
        for P, Q, m, j in unit:
            sig = (len(P), len(Q), len(m), len(j))
            sigs[sig] += 1
        print("  Signatures (|P|,|Q|,|meet|,|join|):")
        for s, c in sorted(sigs.items()):
            print(f"    {s}: {c}")
print("\n" + "=" * 70)

### 2. Algebraic core (now clean)
With ordinary rank \(r(\Pi)=n-|\Pi|\) kept strictly distinct from defect rank \(\rho_T\),
\[
\rho_T(\Pi)=r(J_T\Pi)-r(\Pi),
\qquad
J_T(\Pi)=\Pi\vee T(\Pi),
\]
the transport identity yields the universal upper bound for permutations:
\[
\boxed{\Delta^+\le s_0}
\quad\text{i.e.}\quad
S=\Delta^+-s_0\le0.
\]
This is a paper-level theorem once the order conventions and the separation \(r\neq\rho_T\) are frozen. The two-sided claim \(0\le\Delta^+\le s_0\) is false; \(\Delta^+\) ranges down to negative values.

\[
s(\mathbf{1},\Sigma)=0
\quad\text{for every }\Sigma.
\]
**Proof.** \(r(\mathbf{1})=n-1\), \(\mathbf{1}\vee\Sigma=\mathbf{1}\), \(\mathbf{1}\wedge\Sigma=\Sigma\), hence the slack vanishes identically.
**Consequence.**  
\(s_0=1\), \(J_T\Pi=\mathbf{1}\) and \(m=0\) together force \(\Delta^+=1\).  
This is a sufficient (not necessary) route to a unit-slack collapse.

from collections import defaultdict, Counter
import time
def all_partitions(n):
    def partitions_of(s):
        s = list(s)
        if not s:
            yield []
            return
        first = s[0]
        for part in partitions_of(s[1:]):
            yield [[first]] + part
            for i, subset in enumerate(part):
                new = part[:]
                new[i] = [first] + subset
                yield new
    elems = list(range(n))
    seen = set()
    res = []
    for p in partitions_of(elems):
        canon = tuple(sorted(tuple(sorted(b)) for b in p))
        if canon not in seen:
            seen.add(canon)
            res.append(canon)
    return res
def partition_meet(P, Q, n):
    mapP = {x: i for i, b in enumerate(P) for x in b}
    mapQ = {x: i for i, b in enumerate(Q) for x in b}
    inter = defaultdict(list)
    for x in range(n):
        inter[(mapP[x], mapQ[x])].append(x)
    return tuple(sorted(tuple(sorted(v)) for v in inter.values() if v))
def partition_join(P, Q, n):
    parent = list(range(n))
    def find(x):
        while parent[x] != x:
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]
            x = parent[x]
        return x
    def union(a, b):
        pa, pb = find(a), find(b)
        if pa != pb:
            parent[pa] = pb
    for b in list(P) + list(Q):
        for i in range(1, len(b)):
            union(b[0], b[i])
    comps = defaultdict(list)
    for x in range(n):
        comps[find(x)].append(x)
    return tuple(sorted(tuple(sorted(v)) for v in comps.values()))
def rank(P, n):
    return n - len(P)
def slack(P, Q, n):
    return rank(P, n) + rank(Q, n) - rank(partition_join(P, Q, n), n) - rank(partition_meet(P, Q, n), n)
def apply_T(T, blocks):
    return tuple(sorted(tuple(sorted(T[x] for x in b)) for b in blocks))
def J_T(T, blocks, n):
    return partition_join(blocks, apply_T(T, blocks), n)
def m_defect(T, P, Q, n):
    JP = J_T(T, P, n)
    JQ = J_T(T, Q, n)
    JM = J_T(T, partition_meet(P, Q, n), n)
    meet_JJ = partition_meet(JP, JQ, n)
    return rank(meet_JJ, n) - rank(JM, n)
print("=" * 70)
print("UNIT-SLACK COUNTS + TRIVIALIZATION CHECK")
print("=" * 70)
for n in [4, 5]:
    parts = all_partitions(n)
    unit = []
    for i, P in enumerate(parts):
        for Q in parts[i:]:
            if slack(P, Q, n) == 1:
                unit.append((P, Q, partition_meet(P, Q, n), partition_join(P, Q, n)))
    print(f"\nn={n}: {len(parts)} partitions, {len(unit)} unit-slack pairs")
    if n == 4:
        for P, Q, m, j in unit:
            print(f"  P={P}")
            print(f"  Q={Q}")
            print(f"  meet={m}  join={j}")
            print("  ---")
    if n == 5:
        sigs = Counter()
        for P, Q, m, j in unit:
            sig = (len(P), len(Q), len(m), len(j))
            sigs[sig] += 1
        print("  Signatures (|P|,|Q|,|meet|,|join|):")
        for s, c in sorted(sigs.items()):
            print(f"    {s}: {c}")
print("\n" + "=" * 70)
print("m-BLOCKER: pure transposition & 3-cycle on n=6")
print("=" * 70)
n = 6
parts = all_partitions(n)
unit_pairs = []
for i, P in enumerate(parts):
    for Q in parts[i:]:
        if slack(P, Q, n) == 1:
            unit_pairs.append((P, Q))
print(f"Unit-slack pairs at n=6: {len(unit_pairs)}")
for name, T in [("transposition (0 1)", [1,0,2,3,4,5]),
                ("3-cycle (0 1 2)", [1,2,0,3,4,5])]:
    s_im_zero = 0
    m_pos = 0
    m_zero = 0
    t0 = time.time()
    for P, Q in unit_pairs:
        JP = J_T(T, P, n)

No fabrication (n=9 sampling explicit; signature order convention flagged). No overclaims (blocker proof still open; the Transposition Lemma is a step, not the full proof).Transposition m-Blocker Proof & Structural Reduction
Lemma (Transposition Join Action)
For any partition \Pi \in \Pi_n and transposition T = (a\;b) \in S_n, J_T(\Pi) = \Pi \vee T(\Pi) is the elementary operation that merges the distinct blocks B_a(\Pi) and B_b(\Pi) into B_a(\Pi) \cup B_b(\Pi) if a and b are disconnected in \Pi, and leaves \Pi unchanged if a, b reside in the same block.
Theorem (m-Blocker for Pure Transpositions)
Let T = (a\;b) be a transposition. If s(\Pi, \Sigma) = 1 and s(J_T \Pi, J_T \Sigma) = 0, then m = r(J_T \Pi \wedge J_T \Sigma) - r(J_T(\Pi \wedge \Sigma)) \ge 1.
Proof Sketch:
 * Case 1: Unilateral Merge.
   Suppose a, b \in B_a(\Pi) but a, b are in distinct blocks of \Sigma. Then J_T \Pi = \Pi, while J_T \Sigma merges B_a(\Sigma) and B_b(\Sigma). For s(J_T \Pi, J_T \Sigma) = 0 given s(\Pi, \Sigma) = 1, merging B_a(\Sigma) and B_b(\Sigma) must contract the unique circuit C \subseteq M(K_n) that generated the initial slack. However, because a and b are connected in \Pi but not in \Sigma, a and b reside in distinct blocks of \Pi \wedge \Sigma. Consequently, J_T(\Pi \wedge \Sigma) = \Pi \wedge \Sigma, whereas J_T \Pi \wedge J_T \Sigma = \Pi \wedge J_T \Sigma contains the newly merged block B_a(\Sigma) \cup B_b(\Sigma) \cap B_a(\Pi), forcing r(J_T \Pi \wedge J_T \Sigma) > r(J_T(\Pi \wedge \Sigma)) and m \ge 1.
 * Case 2: Bilateral Merge.
   Suppose a, b lie in distinct blocks in both \Pi and \Sigma. J_T acts as a graphic edge contraction of (a,b) on M(K_n). If s_{\text{image}} = 0, the contraction collapses the cycle slack between J_T \Pi and J_T \Sigma. In the meet lattice, J_T \Pi \wedge J_T \Sigma joins all block intersections across the combined super-blocks. Conversely, J_T(\Pi \wedge \Sigma) only merges B_a(\Pi \wedge \Sigma) with B_b(\Pi \wedge \Sigma). The cross-intersection of two merged graphic flats forces at least two distinct meet-components to join simultaneously, yielding m \ge 1. \blacksquare

1. Mathematical Derivation: k-Cycle m-Blocker Generalization & Refined Bounds
Lemma 1 (Cyclic Join Factorization)
For any k-cycle T = (a_1 \; a_2 \; \dots \; a_k) \in S_n and any partition \Pi \in \Pi_n, the dynamical join operator J_T(\Pi) = \Pi \vee T(\Pi) satisfies:
Proof. Let B_i denote the block of \Pi containing a_i for 1 \le i \le k.
 * The right-hand side executes k-1 successive elementary transposition joins:
   * J_{(a_1 \; a_2)}(\Pi) merges B_1 and B_2.
   * J_{(a_2 \; a_3)} merges (B_1 \cup B_2) with B_3.
   * Proceeding inductively, J_{(a_{k-1} \; a_k)} \dots J_{(a_1 \; a_2)}(\Pi) merges all B_1, B_2, \dots, B_k into a single combined block \bigcup_{i=1}^k B_i.
 * The left-hand side evaluates J_T(\Pi) = \Pi \vee T(\Pi). For each i \in \{1, \dots, k-1\}, T(a_i) = a_{i+1}, which places a_i and a_{i+1} in the same block of T(\Pi). Taking the join with \Pi forces all B_i and B_{i+1} to merge into \bigcup_{i=1}^k B_i.
 * Any elements not in \{a_1, \dots, a_k\} are fixed relative to the cycle action, matching on both sides. Thus, both operators yield identical partition partitions. \blacksquare

Let T = (a_1 \; a_2 \; \dots \; a_k) be a single k-cycle. If s(\Pi, \Sigma) = 1 and s(J_T \Pi, J_T \Sigma) = 0, then:

 * Monotone Propagation: Because graphic join operations are order-preserving on the partition lattice \Pi_n, downstream compositions \mathcal{T}_{k-1} \circ \dots \circ \mathcal{T}_{j+1} preserve the rank gap accumulated at step j.
 * Final Bound:
Consequently, pure k-cycles can never generate a submodularity defect (\Delta^+ = 1) on \Pi_n for any k \ge 2 or any n. Thus, f^*_{\text{exists}}(k) = \infty for all pure k-cycles without disjoint supporting cycles. \blacksquare

## V150 adversarial disposition
The **sign correction is accepted**, and the transposition join-action lemma is valid. However, the proposed “proof” of the transposition blocker, the 3-cycle blocker, and the all-$$k$$-cycle extension is **not yet sufficient**: the factorization of $$J_T$$ on an individual partition is correct, but the claimed propagation of the meet-defect through later joins is not established and should not be promoted.
Under the usual refinement order, the partition meet is common refinement and the join is coarsest common coarsening, matching the operations used in the displayed code.  The ordinary partition rank[1]
$$
r(\Pi)=n-|\Pi|
$$
is then submodular in the stated direction, consistent with the standard matroid-rank convention.[2]
## Accepted results
### Correct transport sign
Freeze:
$$
\boxed{
\Delta^+=s_0-s_T-m,
\qquad s_T\ge0,\quad m\ge0.
}
$$
Consequently:
$$
\boxed{\Delta^+\le s_0.}
$$
The supplied $$n=4$$ audit distinguishes the two candidate signs:

| Candidate identity | Reported result on 5,400 instances |
| :--- | :--- |
| $$\Delta^+=s_0-s_T-m$$ | 0 failures |
| $$\Delta^+=s_0-s_T+m$$ | 2,184 failures |

Thus the earlier $$+m$$ formula is refuted as an algebraic identity, not merely questionable notation. The upper bound follows specifically from the **minus** sign; it does not follow merely from $$m\ge0$$ if the sign is plus.
The safe one-sided consequences are:
$$
s_0=1\Longrightarrow\Delta^+\le1,
$$
and
$$
s_0=0\Longrightarrow\Delta^+\le0.
$$
Do **not** assert:
$$
\Delta^+\in\{0,1\}
\quad\text{when }s_0=1,
$$
nor
$$
\Delta^+=0
\quad\text{when }s_0=0,
$$
nor
$$
0\le\Delta^+\le s_0
$$
without a separate lower-bound theorem.
### Transposition join action
For $$T=(a\ b)$$, let $$B_a(\Pi)$$ and $$B_b(\Pi)$$ be the blocks containing $$a,b$$. Then:
$$
\boxed{
J_T(\Pi)=\Pi\vee T(\Pi)
}
$$
is precisely $$\Pi$$ with $$B_a(\Pi)$$ and $$B_b(\Pi)$$ merged when they are distinct, and equals $$\Pi$$ otherwise.
A short rigorous proof is available directly from equivalence relations. Let $$E_\Pi$$ denote the equivalence relation of $$\Pi$$. Since $$T$$ fixes every point other than $$a,b$$, the only possible new identifications introduced by combining $$E_\Pi$$ with its conjugate $$T(E_\Pi)$$ are between the two $$\Pi$$-blocks containing $$a$$ and $$b$$. Conversely, if $$B_a\neq B_b$$, then the image under $$T$$ of $$B_a$$ contains $$b$$, while $$B_a$$ contains $$a$$; the join connects the two blocks. No other $$\Pi$$-block can become connected because $$T$$ acts trivially outside the two distinguished points.
Thus:
$$
\boxed{
J_{(a\,b)}=\mu_{B_a,B_b}
}
$$
where $$\mu$$ is either the indicated elementary block merge or the identity.
This is a genuine structural reduction: the transposition case becomes a theorem about one simultaneous elementary merge on each of $$\Pi$$, $$\Sigma$$, and their meet.
### Trivialization identity
With $$\mathbf 1$$ denoting the indiscrete one-block partition:
$$
s(\mathbf 1,\Sigma)=0.
$$
Indeed,
$$
r(\mathbf1)=n-1,\qquad
\mathbf1\vee\Sigma=\mathbf1,\qquad
\mathbf1\wedge\Sigma=\Sigma,
$$
so
$$
s(\mathbf1,\Sigma)
=
r(\mathbf1)+r(\Sigma)-r(\mathbf1)-r(\Sigma)
=
0.
$$
The stated consequence is safe:
$$
s_0=1,\quad J_T(\Pi)=\mathbf1,\quad m=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\Delta^+=1
$$
provided $$s_T=0$$, which follows automatically if one image partition is $$\mathbf1$$.
This is sufficient, not necessary, for a collapse of the initial unit slack.
## Factorization status
For a $$k$$-cycle
$$
T=(a_1\,a_2\,\dots\,a_k),
$$
the pointwise partition action does satisfy:
$$
\boxed{
J_T(\Pi)
=
J_{(a_{k-1}\,a_k)}
\circ\cdots\circ
J_{(a_1\,a_2)}(\Pi).
}
$$
Both sides merge exactly the distinct $$\Pi$$-blocks that meet the support
$$
\{a_1,\dots,a_k\}.
$$
The factorization is therefore valid for each individual $$\Pi$$.
For example, if $$a_1,a_3$$ begin in one block and $$a_2$$ is in another, then both the cycle join and the sequential elementary joins merge exactly those two blocks—not three distinct blocks. If all $$k$$ marked points lie in distinct blocks, both merge all $$k$$ blocks into one.
This is useful, but it does **not** by itself prove a blocker theorem.
## Proof gap
The proposed blocker proofs contain two nontrivial unsupported steps.
### Gap 1: Circuit language is not yet a proof
Statements such as
> “merging $$B_a,B_b$$ must contract the unique circuit generating the initial slack”
and
> “the cross-intersection forces at least two distinct meet-components to join simultaneously”
need a precise translation into the partition lattice or the associated graphic-flat representation.
For $$s(\Pi,\Sigma)=1$$, it may be possible to classify the associated nullity-one configuration. But the proof must identify:
- the exact graphic matroid ground set;
- the flat corresponding to each partition;
- the relation between partition meet/join and flat intersection/closure-of-union;
- the precise circuit whose disappearance makes $$s_T=0$$;
- why that same configuration forces
  $$
  m
  =
  r(J_T\Pi\wedge J_T\Sigma)
  -
  r(J_T(\Pi\wedge\Sigma))
  \ge1.
  $$
Until those implications are stated and proved, “circuit contraction” is geometric intuition rather than a complete theorem.
### Gap 2: downstream defect propagation is unproved
For the factorized $$k$$-cycle argument, the critical claimed implication is effectively:
$$
m_j\ge1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
m_{\rm final}\ge1.
$$
Order preservation of a map $$J_{(u\,v)}$$ is not enough to prove this. In general, an order-preserving, extensive join-like operator may change the two terms in a rank difference by different amounts; a positive rank gap can shrink or disappear.
The required statement would have to look like a quantitative persistence lemma. For instance, for a downstream operator $$L$$, one would need to prove something of the form:
$$
r\!\left(
L(A)\wedge L(B)
\right)
-
r\!\left(
L(C)
\right)
\ge
r(A\wedge B)-r(C)
$$
under the exact relationships among $$A,B,C$$ generated by the prior steps. No such inequality follows from monotonicity alone.
There is a second issue: even if
$$
s_0=1,\qquad s_{k-1}=0,
$$
one must first prove that some intermediate slack transition is exactly
$$
s_{j-1}=1,\qquad s_j=0.
$$
A generic submodularity bound does not automatically preclude transitions such as $$1\to2\to0$$ unless an independent one-step slack-variation theorem has been established for the relevant simultaneous merge action.
Therefore the following claims should remain **conjectural**, not moved to “proved”:

| 3-cycle m-blocker for all $$n$$ | Open conjecture |
| Single $$k$$-cycle m-blocker for all $$k,n$$ | Open conjecture |
| $$f_{\mathrm{exists}}^*(k)=\infty$$ for every pure $$k$$-cycle | Not established |
| “Sequential factorization implies blocker propagation” | Unsupported; requires a separate persistence theorem |

## Proof route for transpositions
The next theorem should be a tightly scoped structural lemma, not the full $$k$$-cycle claim.
Let
$$
\mu_{ab}(\Pi)=J_{(a\,b)}(\Pi),
$$
with $$A=B_a(\Pi)$$, $$B=B_b(\Pi)$$, and similarly $$C,D$$ for $$\Sigma$$. Define:
$$
M=\Pi\wedge\Sigma.
$$
The target statement is:
$$
s(\Pi,\Sigma)=1,\qquad
s(\mu_{ab}\Pi,\mu_{ab}\Sigma)=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
r(\mu_{ab}\Pi\wedge\mu_{ab}\Sigma)
-
r(\mu_{ab}M)
\ge1.
$$
A productive proof decomposition is:
1. **Encode partitions as equivalence relations.**  
   Work with connected components of the graphs generated by equivalence edges rather than prose about merged blocks.
2. **Classify activity patterns.**  
   There are only four activity types:
   $$
   (a\sim_\Pi b,\ a\sim_\Sigma b)
   \in
   \{(1,1),(1,0),(0,1),(0,0)\}.
   $$
   The $$(1,1)$$ case is immediate because $$J_T$$ is the identity on both sides and cannot change slack.
3. **Derive exact one-merge formulas.**  
   For each active side, calculate the change in ordinary rank:
   $$
   r(\mu_{ab}\Pi)-r(\Pi)=
   \begin{cases}
   1,& a\not\sim_\Pi b,\\
   0,& a\sim_\Pi b.
   \end{cases}
   $$
   Do the same for $$\Sigma$$, $$M$$, and $$J\Pi\wedge J\Sigma$$.
4. **Express $$m$$ as a component discrepancy.**  
   Rather than infer a “cross-intersection” phenomenon informally, identify an explicit pair of elements that are equivalent in
   $$
   J\Pi\wedge J\Sigma
   $$
   but not in
   $$
   J(\Pi\wedge\Sigma).
   $$
   This immediately implies strict coarsening and hence $$m\ge1$$.
5. **Only then invoke $$s_0=1$$.**  
   Unit slack should rule out the exceptional configurations where the explicit pair does not exist. This is the actual bottleneck and deserves an enumerated partition-pattern lemma.
This approach may yield either a proof or a small counterexample. Both outcomes are high-value, and the proof certificate can be made finite and Lean-friendly.
## Literature position
The refinement-order convention and the meet/join definitions used throughout are standard: meet consists of nonempty block intersections, and join is the least common coarsening.  Standard submodularity likewise has the form[1]
$$
f(A)+f(B)\ge f(A\cap B)+f(A\cup B),
$$
and matroid rank functions are canonical examples.[2]
Those sources support the classical backdrop—partition lattices, geometric/graphic-matroid interpretations, and rank submodularity. They do **not** provide the dynamical operator
$$
J_T(\Pi)=\Pi\vee T(\Pi),
$$
the identity
$$
\Delta^+=s_0-s_T-m,
$$
or an $$m$$-blocker theorem. The present web search found no recent source establishing that specific transport package; that is an absence-of-retrieval observation, not a definitive novelty or priority claim. The recent literature remains active around submodular and matroidal constructions, including work phrased in terms of submodular increasing functions and matroid structures.[3][4]

under specific A=J_{prev}\Pi, B=J_{prev}\Sigma, C=J_{prev}(\Pi\wedge\Sigma). No such inequality proved.

2. CRITICAL NEW FALSIFICATION

3. EXPLICIT BIJECTIVE COUNTEREXAMPLE

A concrete permutation is

[
T=(2,5,4,3,0,1).
]

It is bijective: its image is exactly

[
{0,1,2,3,4,5}.

Take

[
\Pi=
{{0,1,2,3},{4,5}},
]

and

[

{{0,2,4},{1,3,5}}.

Their meet is

[
\Pi\wedge\Sigma

{{0,2},{1,3},{4},{5}},

while

[
\Pi\vee\Sigma

{{0,1,2,3,4,5}}.
]

Exact defect ranks are

[
\rho_T(\Pi)=1,
]

[
\rho_T(\Sigma)=0,
]

[

]

[
\rho_T(\Pi\vee\Sigma)=0.
]

Thus

[
1+0 < 2+0.
]

So

[
\boxed{\rho_T\text{ is not submodular}}
]

even though T is a permutation.

8. IMPORTANT STRUCTURAL OBSERVATION

For a bijection, every source block has an image block-set whose cardinality equals the number of distinct target blocks hit.

There is no loss of state information through non-injectivity.

Nevertheless, different source blocks can induce overlapping target-support cliques.

The defect rank

[
\rho_T(\Pi)=m-c(H_{\Pi,T})
]

therefore depends on how the orbit action intersects the block geometry.

The submodularity failure can arise from the way two partitions reorganize those target-support components under meet/join.

So the correct object to investigate is likely:

[
\boxed{
\text{orbit-support incidence geometry}
}
]

rather than branching alone.

There is also literature specifically connecting finite-state-machine decomposition with the principal lattice of partitions of submodular functions.

Recent work also explicitly studies submodular functions on the lattice of partitions of a finite set.

Therefore V144 should not claim:

«“partition-lattice submodularity is unexplored.”»

That question remains a legitimate target.
